title: Responsible AI: inclusiveness, transparency and accountability
learningObjective: Describe considerations for inclusiveness, transparency and accountability in an AI solution.
foundation: Inclusiveness: design AI so that everyone can benefit and take part, including people with disabilities, different languages, and limited connectivity.
Transparency: people should know when they are dealing with AI, what it can and can't do, and, where possible, why it reached a result.
Accountability: people, not the AI, are responsible for AI systems. Someone owns the system, decisions are governed, and humans can step in.
engineer: Inclusiveness practices: support assistive technologies (screen readers, captions, keyboard navigation), offer several input and output modes (speech, text, images), localise languages, design for low bandwidth, and test with diverse users including people with disabilities. Microsoft's inclusive design guidance applies.

Transparency practices: disclose AI-generated content and AI interactions; document intended uses, capabilities and limitations (Microsoft publishes Transparency Notes for its AI services); provide explanations or contributing factors for decisions (interpretability); cite sources for grounded answers; add content credentials (provenance) to generated images.

Accountability practices: name owners; set up governance (review boards, impact assessments, Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard as a model); keep audit logs; provide appeal or feedback channels; maintain human oversight with the ability to override or switch off; comply with laws and industry standards.
These principles work together: a transparent system makes accountability possible; inclusive testing reveals fairness problems.

example.title: A city services chatbot
body: The city's assistant accepts voice and text in five languages and works with screen readers (inclusiveness).

Every answer says it was AI-generated and links to its sources, and a published notice explains what it can't do (transparency). A named service owner reviews complaints monthly, and staff can disable it instantly (accountability).

prerequisites: An Azure subscription with access to Microsoft Foundry (ai.azure.com)
limits: Model availability differs by region and deployment type
Deployments have tokens-per-minute (TPM) rate limits and quota per subscription and region
portal: Foundry portal > model card: intended uses and limitations (transparency).
Foundry portal > Monitoring and tracing: keep records of agent runs for review (accountability).
Speech playground: test voice input and captions (inclusiveness).

troubleshooting.symptom: Users don't realise answers come from AI and trust them blindly.
troubleshooting.fix: Label AI-generated content and explain limitations.

troubleshooting.symptom: Nobody can say who approved an AI feature after an incident.
troubleshooting.fix: Assign owners and require reviews for high-impact uses.

comparisons.difference: Transparency includes disclosure and documentation; explainability is one part: why a specific result was produced.
Accountability is about people and governance; reliability is about the system behaving correctly.

misconceptions.myth: Transparency means publishing the model's source code.
misconceptions.reality: It means people understand the system's use, limits and outputs.

misconceptions.myth: If the AI made the decision, nobody is accountable.

misconceptions.reality: It also covers language, culture, connectivity and more.

architectureDecisions: Publish what your system can and can't do.
Name an owner and keep a human able to override.
